note: Recent papers in anaesthesia and critical care from PubMed, summarised in plain words. Read the original before changing practice.

items.title: Inhaled anesthetics and severe neurologic complications in individuals with Venezuelan maternal ancestry carrying the mitochondrial MT-ND4 m.11232 T > C variant: a systematic review.
items.summary: This review pulled together case reports and lab work since 2021 on previously well children and adults of Venezuelan maternal descent who failed to wake up, developed basal ganglia damage and often died after routine general anaesthesia, mostly with sevoflurane. A mitochondrial complex I variant (MT-ND4 m.11232T>C) is the leading suspect, and in patient cells sevoflurane, but not propofol, sharply impaired complex I function. How common the variant is and how risky each agent truly is remain unknown, so the authors favour avoiding volatiles in at-risk patients.
items.why: A new pharmacogenetic anaesthesia hazard worth knowing alongside malignant hyperthermia: a good reminder to ask about unexplained anaesthetic deaths in maternal relatives and to have a TIVA plan ready.

items.title: National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Care for Adults With Suspected Sepsis in the Emergency Department: A Hybrid Type 1 Effectiveness-Implementation Stepped-Wedge Randomized Controlled Trial Pilot Study (NEWS-1 TRIPS).
items.summary: In four Hong Kong emergency departments, about 200 adults with infection and a NEWS-2 score of 5 or more were enrolled in a stepped-wedge pilot where a high score automatically triggered the Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle. Lactate, blood cultures and early antibiotics were done more often, but full bundle completion reached only 56%, and 30-day mortality did not differ significantly (3.9% usual care vs 9.2% with the new pathway; the trial was far too small to judge). The authors conclude a full-scale trial is feasible but needs many more patients.
items.why: Shows that a simple, free bedside score can push teams towards faster sepsis basics, but also that the Hour-1 Bundle is hard to deliver in a busy casualty, a familiar problem in Indian emergency departments and ICUs.

items.title: Effect of discontinuing antihypertensives on perioperative hypotension in older patients before non-cardiac surgery: multicentre, randomised, double blind, controlled trial.
items.summary: About 2000 patients aged 60-80 on an ACE inhibitor or ARB, having non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia at five Chinese centres, were given either their usual morning dose or an identical placebo capsule. Skipping the dose cut hypotension needing treatment from 46% to 31% (adjusted OR 0.52) and reduced vasopressor use, with no difference in 30-day complications or deaths.
items.why: A large blinded trial that settles a daily pre-op question: holding the ACEi/ARB on the morning of surgery costs nothing and means less post-induction hypotension, and it is a likely viva topic.

items.title: Sigh ventilation versus conventional protective ventilation in cardiac surgery: a proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial.
items.summary: In 192 adults having elective on-pump cardiac surgery, low tidal volume ventilation alone was compared with the same strategy plus one large 'sigh' breath (plateau about 35 cmH2O) every 6 minutes. The sigh group had better compliance, lower driving pressure, and a higher SpO2/FiO2 ratio in the first hour after extubation (about 380 vs 338), with less severe respiratory failure and no extra harm.
items.why: Periodic sighs need only a ventilator setting, so this is an easy-to-try add-on to lung-protective ventilation, though the oxygenation gain was small and needs confirming in bigger trials.

items.title: Consensus on the definition, components, and grading of composite postoperative pulmonary complication outcomes (PrECiSIOn): insights from an international Delphi expert panel.
items.summary: An international panel of 44 experts, with input from patients, used a Delphi process to agree on what should count as a postoperative pulmonary complication. They grouped components into four domains (symptoms, diagnoses, therapies, outcomes) and ranked them by severity so trials can use graded composite outcomes; no agreement was reached on how long follow-up should last.
items.why: Useful for anyone planning a thesis or reading PPC trials, since it gives a standard, severity-weighted way to define the outcome.

items.title: Global Prevalence of Obstetric Causes of Critical Illness in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.summary: Pooling 50 studies covering over 7.7 million obstetric patients in 20 countries, about 1 in 100 pregnant or postpartum women needed ICU care, rising to roughly 4% in low-income countries. Most admissions had direct obstetric causes, mainly hypertensive disorders (27%) and haemorrhage (23%); a third needed respiratory or transfusion support and 8.5% died.
items.why: Led by an ICMR team, it underlines that PPH and pre-eclampsia drive obstetric ICU load in settings like India, which shapes how obstetric HDU and ICU beds are planned.

items.title: New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review of In-Hospital and Post-Discharge Outcomes.
items.summary: A Bayesian meta-analysis of 54 studies (about 368,000 ICU patients) found that around 11% developed atrial fibrillation for the first time during critical illness. These patients had roughly double the risk of stroke or other thromboembolism after discharge (about 7% absolute), about a quarter were later diagnosed with ongoing AF, yet only about a third received anticoagulation.
items.why: Shows that ICU-onset AF is not always transient, so it is worth flagging in discharge summaries for follow-up and anticoagulation review.

items.title: Early albumin use and mortality in critically III children with severe hypoalbuminemia: a target trial emulation study.
items.summary: Using records of 1649 children in a Chinese PICU whose first albumin was below 30 g/L, the authors mimicked a trial of giving human albumin within 24 hours versus not. Early albumin was linked to lower 7-day mortality (HR 0.42) but not 28-day mortality, and the signal faded with looser albumin cut-offs or later treatment.
items.why: Albumin is expensive in Indian PICUs, and this observational signal is not strong enough to justify routine use without a proper randomised trial.

items.title: Volume Guarantee Versus Manual Tidal Volume Monitoring During High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation in Neonates: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.summary: At AIIMS Rishikesh, 60 neonates who failed conventional ventilation were rescued with high-frequency oscillation using either automatic volume guarantee or careful manual tidal volume adjustment. Abnormal CO2 at 1 hour was similar (50% vs 43%), as were CO2 trends, cerebral oxygenation, duration of support and complications.
items.why: An Indian trial suggesting that close manual tidal volume monitoring can match volume guarantee, which matters where oscillators with that feature are not available.

items.title: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
items.summary: In a single-centre pilot, 100 surgical and trauma ICU adults who already had delirium got either oral guanfacine 2 mg each night or a placebo for up to two weeks. The trial ran smoothly (full adherence and follow-up), and guanfacine patients had slightly more days alive without delirium or coma (median 2 vs 1), though this lost significance after adjustment. No blood pressure or heart rate problems were seen, and ICU stay and ventilation time were similar.
items.why: Guanfacine is a cheap oral alpha-2 agonist, so if a larger trial confirms benefit it could be an affordable alternative to dexmedetomidine for ICU delirium in Indian units.

items.title: Videolaryngoscopy vs. direct laryngoscopy for tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors (VILARE): a pragmatic multicentre randomised trial.
items.summary: About 1000 adults intubated by supervised anaesthesia residents were randomised to a videolaryngoscope or a direct laryngoscope for the first attempt. First-pass success was higher with videolaryngoscopy (79% vs 70%), with better glottic views, less reported difficulty and fewer complications (8% vs 18%), and no meaningful difference in intubation time.
items.why: Strong support for making videolaryngoscopy the default first device when trainees intubate.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of oliceridine versus remifentanil for analgesia in mechanically ventilated critically ill adults (CO-ROAM): a multicenter, assessor-blinded, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial.
items.summary: In 304 ventilated ICU adults across 19 Chinese ICUs, oliceridine (a G-protein-biased mu-opioid agonist) kept patients in the target analgesia range as well as remifentanil. It caused fewer mild-to-moderate drug reactions, no respiratory depression (vs about 5% with remifentanil, and 0% vs 8% after extubation) and lower costs; ventilation time, ICU stay and 28-day mortality were similar.
items.why: A possible opioid option with a better respiratory safety profile for ICU analgesia, though availability in India may be limited.

items.title: Sugammadex versus neostigmine for neuromuscular blockade reversal in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
items.summary: This update of the 2017 Cochrane review pooled 165 trials (about 19,000 adults). Sugammadex 2 mg/kg reversed blockade to TOF ratio above 0.9 about 10 minutes faster than neostigmine and probably lowered the chance of any adverse event (RR 0.72), including residual block, desaturation, atelectasis, bradycardia and urinary retention. Certainty was moderate and many trials had risk of bias.
items.why: As sugammadex gets cheaper, this is the most complete summary of what it actually gains you over neostigmine.

items.title: Individualized mean arterial pressure during cardiac surgery The OPTIPAM Randomized Clinical Trial.
items.summary: In 10 French centres, cardiac surgery patients on bypass were targeted either to within 10% of their own baseline MAP or to a standard MAP of 65 mmHg or more. The trial was stopped early (172 patients) because bleeding complications were higher with individualised targets (18% vs 3%); death, AKI or neurological complications were not reduced (32% vs 29%).
items.why: A safety signal: pushing pressure higher with vasopressors during cardiac surgery may increase bleeding without clear benefit.

items.title: Quality of Recovery After Primary Breast Cancer Surgery: A Randomized, Two-Centre, Triple-Blinded Trial Comparing Erector Spinae Plane Block and Intravenous Lidocaine Infusion Within a Multimodal Analgesia Framework.
items.summary: Eighty women having breast cancer surgery with standard multimodal analgesia received either an ultrasound-guided erector spinae plane block or an intraoperative lidocaine infusion. Quality of recovery at 24 hours (QoR-15), pain and opioid use were similar and low in both groups, with no block- or lidocaine-related adverse events.
items.why: IV lidocaine may be a practical alternative when a block isn't feasible, at least within a good multimodal plan.

items.title: Intravenous Lidocaine in Liver Surgery ‒ A Randomized Double-Blind Trial.
items.summary: In 124 patients having minor liver resection, a lidocaine bolus (1.5 mg/kg) plus infusion (1.5 mg/kg/h until 1 h after surgery) did not reduce 24-hour opioid use compared with placebo. Pain scores were lower only early after surgery; recovery scores and adverse events were similar, and plasma levels stayed below toxic range after brief early peaks in two patients.
items.why: Lidocaine infusion looks safe in minor liver surgery but adds little beyond the first hours.

items.title: Efficacy and Safety of Ulinastatin in the Treatment of Patients with Sepsis: The ADJUST Trial.
items.summary: In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 335 adults with sepsis, ulinastatin 400,000 IU every 8 hours for up to 10 days did not change 28-day mortality (about 23% in both groups) or other outcomes. Adverse events were more frequent with ulinastatin (57% vs 43%).
items.why: Ulinastatin is used in some Indian ICUs for sepsis; this trial does not support routine use.

items.title: Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
items.summary: Pooling four RCTs (about 1500 ICU adults with metabolic acidosis), IV sodium bicarbonate showed no clear survival benefit (RR 0.94) but a high probability of reducing the need for renal replacement therapy (RR 0.74, 97% probability of benefit). No consistent safety concern was seen.
items.why: Bicarbonate may spare some patients dialysis even if it doesn't save lives; who benefits most is still open.

items.title: Normocapnia Versus Mild Hypercapnia During Lung Protective Ventilation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Target Trial Emulation.
items.summary: Using data from seven ARDS Network/PETAL trials, the authors compared aiming for normal PaCO2 (35-45, by raising respiratory rate) with tolerating mild hypercapnia (50-55) during low tidal volume ventilation. 90-day mortality was identical (29% in each group, 292 per arm), including in older and obese patients.
items.why: Supports permissive mild hypercapnia; no need to chase normal CO2 with high respiratory rates. Observational design, so interpret cautiously.

items.title: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units.
items.summary: In six medical ICUs in Bhubaneswar (about 1000 ventilated patients), adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standard oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP (about 17-19 per 1000 ventilator-days) or 28-day mortality, and ICU stay was slightly longer with chlorhexidine.
items.why: An Indian trial adding to the evidence that chlorhexidine mouthwash can be dropped from VAP bundles in medical ICUs.

items.title: The effect of intravenous ondansetron on maternal spinal-induced hypotension in preeclamptic patients undergoing caesarean delivery: a randomised, controlled clinical trial.
items.summary: A randomised trial testing whether IV ondansetron reduces spinal-induced hypotension in women with preeclampsia having caesarean delivery. The abstract isn't on PubMed yet, so the results aren't summarised here.
items.why: Directly relevant to obstetric spinal anaesthesia; worth opening the full paper.

items.title: Prophylactic esketamine to reduce postpartum depression in primiparous women: A multicentre, double-blind, randomised clinical trial.
items.summary: A multicentre double-blind trial of prophylactic esketamine to prevent postpartum depression in first-time mothers. The abstract isn't on PubMed yet, so the results aren't summarised here.
items.why: Part of a growing set of trials on perioperative esketamine in obstetrics.
